new_statements.rule_in_words: The dedicated grammar of inscriptional Old Telugu (to 1100 AD) states that the position of the accent is not recoverable from the record ('want of information on accent'); where it invokes accent at all it presupposes the traditional Dravidian pattern - accented radical (first) syllable, unaccented second syllable whose short vowel is syncopated (nilupu > nilp-i, paluku > palk-ina). No positive rule for Old Telugu word stress is given. Sitapati 1936 (p. 525), by contrast, asserts that particular Old Telugu forms (ata'da 'it is only he', ko'landi 'few') carried primary accent on a non-initial short syllable and that 'later Telugu' shifted accent to the first syllable unless the accented syllable had a long vowel; Subbayya 1909's pre-Telugu accent-shift theory is reported by Krishnamurti 1955 ('a system of accentuation, for which we have no evidence') and Subrahmanyam 1983 as disproved.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing for Old Telugu. (Sitapati 1936 describes secondary accent only for modern Telugu compounds and significant final particles.)
new_statements.exceptions: Radhakrishna: none (no rule stated). Sitapati 1936 p.525: Old Telugu,ata'da with final-syllable primary accent and ko'landi with second-syllable accent, later shifted to initial ('koddi); shift blocked when the accented syllable had a long vowel.
new_statements.domain_note: Radhakrishna's only accent-bearing statement concerns word-internal syncope before tense suffixes (word domain, inscriptional spellings); he explicitly says accent, pause and pronunciation of Early Telugu are unknown. Sitapati's Old Telugu forms are cited as isolated words/clitic groups reconstructed from modern reflexes, not from any Old Telugu accent notation.
new_statements.identity_note: Radhakrishna 1971 describes 'Early Telugu (ETe.)' = the language of the Telugu inscriptions from the 4th/5th c. to 1100 AD, i.e. the pre-Nannaya/inscriptional stage that Glottolog's Old Telugu (oldt1249) denotes. Sitapati 1936's 'old Telugu' is used loosely for the earlier/classical literary language as opposed to modern spoken Telugu (modern Telugu = telu1262, already catalogued separately with the Sitapati/Pingali weight-sensitive first-two-syllables rule). Subbayya 1909 and the accent-shift debate concern reconstructed pre-Telugu, not attested Old Telugu.

sources.note: No accent section. p. cv: 'for want of information on accent, pause and pronounciation in ETe.' (accent of Early Telugu not recoverable); p. xcvi, verb-stem alternations: '(3) vowels of the unaccented second syllable are dropped. Eg. nilp-i, nilp-e, palk-ina' (presupposes accented radical/first syllable, unaccented second); p. lxxviii-lxxix reports Subbayya's pre-Telugu 'accent shift from the first to the second syllable' as one account of metathesis, alongside Krishnamurti's non-accentual account.

sources.note: Covers 1401-1900 (Middle/Late Telugu), not the Old Telugu period; no accent/stress section; only a passing remark that some aspiration spellings 'may also mark stress'.

sources.citation: Subrahmanyam, P. S. 1983. Dravidian Comparative Phonology. Annamalainagar: Annamalai University.
sources.note: ch.16 pp.226-230: history of the accent-shift explanation of Telugu-Kui metathesis (Subbayya; Ramaswami Aiyar: 'the normal rule of Dravidian accentuation, viz., that the radical syllables carried with them the primary accent', with transfer to syllables with l/r in Telugu and Kui); Master 1948's objection; follows Krishnamurti 1961 (non-accentual apical displacement). p.6: Subbayya's accent-shift hypothesis listed among conclusions 'later disproved'. Notes TVB secs 1.180ff, 2.9-21 on loss of vowels in unaccented syllables.

sources.note: pp.238-239: in the modern Dravidian languages 'there is, however, stress of a phonetic but not phonemic character'; old-Telugu/pre-Telugu vowel gradation lies in syllable grouping 'rather than in a system of accentuation, for which we have no evidence'; sec.19 (pp.245-246) rejects 'the vague theory of stress-displacement' (Subbayya, Tuttle, L.V.R. Aiyar, Emeneau) for Telugu metathesis/lengthening.

sources.citation: Subbayya, K. V. 1909. A primer of Dravidian phonology. Indian Antiquary 38: 160 ff. (sec. III 'The Great Accent Change', pp. 161-162).
sources.note: 'In Early Primitive Dravidian, as it is even now in Tamil, Malayalam and Canarese, the accent rested on the root or stem syllable, which is almost always the first syllable'; posits a 1st-7th c. AD shift of accent toward the last syllable in his 'North Dravidian' (incl. Telugu, Gondi) to explain Telugu aphaeresis/metathesis. Superseded and refuted (Master 1948, Krishnamurti 1955/1961, Subrahmanyam 1983).
